reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Noah ran to soccer practice. Coach Sam had a big red ball. All the kids wanted it. Noah got there first. He hugged the ball tight.

"My turn," said Noah. He held it all to himself. His friend Leo had no ball at all. Leo sat on the grass. His face looked sad. Noah looked at Leo. Then he looked at the big red ball. He wanted to kick it, but a kick needs two friends.

Noah rolled the ball to Leo. "You can use it too," said Noah. "This is sharing." Leo smiled big. Leo kicked the ball back. Noah kicked it to Leo again. The ball went back and forth, back and forth.

Soon more kids came over. They made a line for turns. Noah waited. He did not grab. When his turn came, Coach Sam gave him a thumbs up. Noah laughed and kicked the ball far. It flew like a bird over the green grass.

After practice, Mom came to get Noah. She held his hand. "I like playing with Leo," said Noah. Mom kissed his head. The sun went down slowly, like an ocean of orange light in the sky. "Can we come back tomorrow?" asked Noah. Mom said, "Yes, we can."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Snow fell all night. Rehmat looked out the kitchen window. "No school today," said Mama. "A snow day!" Rehmat ate her toast. She was hungry for more. Mama gave her a second slice.

Then Rehmat saw Papa by the door. He had a big shovel. He pushed the snow off the path. Swipe, swipe, swipe. Rehmat put on her boots. "Can I help too?" she asked. Papa gave her a small shovel. She pushed one little pile of snow. Then another pile. Then one more. One, two, three.

The path turned brown and clear. Papa said, "Now we can walk without slipping." Just then, the mail carrier came up the path. His boots went tap, tap, tap on the clear ground. He did not slip one bit. "Is that for us?" Rehmat asked. He handed her a small package. Inside was a tiny toy sled. Rehmat laughed and held it up high. "Snow again tomorrow, please!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Charles sat at the dinner table. He wanted the blueberry cake. Mama put it on the shelf. "You can have cake later," she said.

Charles ate his carrots. Then he asked, "Is it later yet?"

"Not yet," said Mama. "Eat your rice first."

Charles ate his rice. He picked up his spoon. He looked at the shelf. "Is it later now?"

Daddy smiled. "Later means some time after now," he said. "Not right away."

Charles wiggled his toe under the table. He took a tiny bite of bread. He looked at the window. The sky turned pink. His plate was empty.

"Now?" he asked.

"Yes, now it is later," said Mama.

She cut a small piece of cake. Charles took a bite. It was sweet and good.

"Tomorrow we can have cake again," said Daddy.

"What is tomorrow?" asked Charles.

"It is the day after today," said Daddy. "Yesterday we had no cake. Today we have cake."

Charles licked his fork. "I like today," he said. Mama laughed and kissed his head.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Raphael was playing house at daycare. He stirred a big red pot. The pot had a thick blue sock inside. "This is soup," he said. His friend Mia had a baby doll. Mia ran fast and the doll fell down. Boom. The doll hit the floor. Mia began to cry. "The baby fell!" she said. Raphael stopped stirring. He looked at the doll. Would the doll cry too? He waited. The doll did not cry. The doll did not feel the bump at all. Dolls cannot really feel, he thought. But maybe the doll could feel a hug, just pretend.

Raphael picked up the doll. "Here comes a hug," he said. He held the doll close. He patted the doll's back, soft and slow. Then he made a little voice. "I am okay now," the doll said. Mia wiped her eyes. She looked at the doll. "Baby is fine?" she asked. "Baby is fine," said Raphael. He gave the doll to Mia. Mia hugged the doll too. Then she hugged Raphael.

"Thank you," said Mia. Raphael ran back to his pot. He took out the thick sock. He put it on the doll's foot. One sock on, one foot bare. "Baby needs a shoe," said Raphael. Mia laughed. She got a small cup. She fed the doll pretend soup, spoon by spoon. The doll got a full tummy, just pretend. Outside the window, a bird went hop, hop, hop. Raphael pointed at it. "Look," he said. "Maybe the bird wants soup too."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
David woke up and saw white everywhere. The sky was gray and soft. "No school today," said Mom. "Snow day!"

David wanted to sled. But the big hill was far away. The road was too deep with snow.

They stood at the window. They waited. David watched and watched.

Then a big truck came. It had a big scoop in front. Mom said, "Look, a snowplow." The snowplow pushed the snow off the road. The road turned black and clear.

"Now we can drive," said Mom.

They drove to the hill. David went down, down, down. He climbed up again. He was careful on the icy step.

"Daddy, watch me!" he called.

Daddy waved. David zoomed down like a little fish in the sea, fast and free.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Elizabeth went to the park with her dad. She saw the big round swing. She wanted to swing high.

Three kids were playing a game near the slide. It was a waiting game. They counted to ten. Then the next kid slid down. Elizabeth asked to play too. A boy named Sam said yes.

Sam slid down first. Then it was Elizabeth's turn. But Sam ran back up fast. "My turn again," he said. The other kids shook their heads. "That is not fair," one girl said. They all stopped playing. They sat on the bench.

Sam looked at the bench. He came back down. "Okay," he said. "We all take turns." The kids came back. Elizabeth found her spot in the line. She counted to ten out loud. Then she slid down, fast and far. "Yay!" she said.

After the game, Dad had a snack ready. It was a little round cake. Elizabeth broke it in two. She gave half to Sam. "Thank you," he said. Then they ran back to the slide, hand in hand.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Emily sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. She looked out the window. She saw a cow. "A cow is an animal," said Mommy. Then Emily saw a dog. The dog was an animal too. At the red light, a little feather floated down. It landed on the car window. "Mommy, look! A soft little feather."

"Who lost it?" asked Emily. "A bird," said Mommy. "Birds have feathers." Emily gasped. "A bird lost its feather! Can we find the bird?" "The bird flew away," said Mommy. "But the feather can be yours." Emily held the feather. It was soft and gray. She tickled her own nose. "Ah-choo!" she said, and they both laughed.

At the next stop, Emily saw a spider on a leaf. "Hello, spider," she said. "Do you have feathers? No, no. You are not a bird." The car went on. Emily saw a toy store with a big teddy bear. She saw a food truck with bananas. Then a small bird flew right by the window. "It's a bird!" said Emily. She held up her feather and waved it. The bird flapped its wings and flew over the trees. Emily kept the feather safe in her little pocket. "Good night, bird," she whispered. "Thanks for my soft gray feather."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa was coming on the train. Bennett wanted to see the train first. He stood on his toes at the platform. He leaned out far to look. Dad held his hand. "Stand back from the edge," said Dad. "We wait until the train stops." Bennett stepped back behind the yellow line. The big train came in. It stopped. The doors opened. Grandpa stepped out with his bag. "Bennett!" he said. They hugged for a long time.

Grandpa said, "Let us try the market today." At the market, they smelled fresh bread. Bennett helped Grandpa pick red apples. They saw a little turtle in a tank. The turtle was slow. Bennett waved at it. Grandpa bought bread, apples, and one small toy turtle for Bennett. They walked home holding hands. "Train tomorrow too?" asked Bennett. "Yes," laughed Grandpa.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
It was Ayla's first day of school. She ran into the big cafeteria. It had long tables and lots of chairs. She counted them. "One, two, three tables!" she said. Then her tummy made a sound. Rumble, rumble. Ayla was hungry. She wanted lunch right now.

"I want to eat," she told her teacher. "We eat at snack time," said the teacher. "Snack time comes after our morning song." So Ayla waited. She sang the morning song. She painted a cat. She built a tower. One block, two blocks, three blocks, four! Then the bell rang. "Snack time!" everyone shouted.

The class walked to the cafeteria. Ayla sat at table one. She opened her bag. Inside was a surprise. A cookie shaped like a star! "I know that star," she said with a big smile. She took a bite. Her tummy felt happy. "Can we come back for lunch?" she asked. "Yes," said the teacher. "A school day has a time for lunch too." Ayla grinned. "I love school days."

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Sarah sat at the big table. She had paper and paints. Mom sat next to her. Sarah dipped her brush in the yellow paint. She painted a big sun. Then she painted a green garden. The garden had little flowers in it.

Sarah wanted to hold her picture up. She grabbed the paper with her hand. Her fingers pressed on the sun. "Oh no," said Sarah. The yellow sun had a smudge. It looked smeary and yucky. Sarah's lip went down. "My sun is messy," she said.

Mom looked at the paper. "The paint was still wet," said Mom. "Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries." Sarah touched the paper again, very gently. Her finger came away yellow. She saw the wet smear on her skin.

"Let's make a new sun," said Mom. Sarah painted a new sun. This time she put her hands in her lap. She looked at the paint. It was shiny and wet. She waited. She sang a little song while she waited. The paint got dull and dry.

Then Sarah picked up the paper. The sun was clean. No smudge at all. The garden was dry too. "I waited!" said Sarah. Mom clapped her hands. "Let's put it on the wall," said Mom. Sarah carried her picture slowly, with two careful hands.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Billie waited at the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was a sunny day, so Billie wore her sun hat. Then gray clouds came. "Is it going to rain?" Billie asked. "Yes," said her mother. She opened a big umbrella.

Rain went tap, tap, tap on top. Billie held her mother's hand. Then the rain stopped. The wind began to blow. "Look at the trees!" said Billie. The trees swayed back and forth. Leaves blew all around the bus stop.

Billie let go of the umbrella handle. She chased a red leaf. It blew left. It blew right. She chased it across the yard. The leaf went round and round. Billie laughed and laughed. Her hat blew off too! She grabbed her hat and held it tight.

"Why do the leaves run away?" Billie asked. "The wind pushes them," said her mother. Billie caught the red leaf at last. She held it up high. Just then snow began to fall. Billie's mother zipped her thick coat up to her chin. "The bus is coming!" said Billie. She waved her leaf at the big yellow bus.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Maeve sat on the big city bus. She held Mama's hand. "My bunny is gone," said Maeve.

Mama looked under the seat. Maeve looked in her bag. No bunny. The bus went bounce, bounce, bounce. Maeve began to cry a little.

"Think," said Mama. "Where did you see bunny last?"

Maeve thought hard. "I had bunny at the window!" she said. "I showed bunny the cars."

Maeve looked at the window seat. There was bunny, sitting straight up by the glass. The sun was on her soft ears.

"Bunny was watching the cars," said Maeve. She gave bunny a big hug.

"You found her," said Mama.

"Yes! I remembered the last place," said Maeve. She waved bunny's paw at a red car going by. Bunny caught the light on her nose, and Maeve giggled all the way home.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Ryan got to daycare and looked out the window. Gray clouds sat over the playground. Little bits of snow began to fall. Miss Amy wore her red sweater and rang the bell.

"Let's count the blocks," said Miss Amy. Ryan counted with his friends. "One, two, three." Then more blocks. "Four, five, six." The pile grew. "Seven, eight, nine." Miss Amy put down one more block. "Ten!"

Ryan wanted to write ten on his paper. He made a nine. That was not ten. He made a one. That was not ten either. He frowned at his paper.

Then he saw the big number card on the wall. Ten had two numbers. There was a 1 first. Then a 0. Ryan wrote a 1. He wrote a 0 right after it. "I made ten!" he said.

Miss Amy smiled. Ryan held up his paper. Outside, the snow fell on the swings.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Lily loved school. At school she counted three things each day. One big clock. One small clock. One sleepy class rabbit.

At lunch, the teacher poured soup. The soup was hot. Lily blew on it slowly. Then she drank her milk. The milk was cold. One, two, three sips, fast.

After lunch came rest time. Lily closed her eyes. The room got dark. When she woke up, the room was still dark. "It's morning!" she wanted to shout. "Time to play!"

But the teacher knelt down. "Look out the window," she said. "It is dark outside. It is still night. Night and day are opposites."

Lily looked. The moon was up. The big clock said rest time was not over. One, two, three more minutes.

Then her friend Ben slid a letter under her mat. It was a picture of the moon. Lily smiled. She touched the class rabbit. His nose felt a little slimy and wet.

The light came back on. "Morning now," said Lily. She hopped up, fast, and ran to the toy cars.

story:
Madison went to the library with her mom. She found a box of toy monkeys. There were ten little monkeys in the box. Madison counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten monkeys sat on the table.

Then she heard a song. A boy was singing in the corner. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed." Madison picked five monkeys. She put them on a book about a park. She sang too. "One fell off and bumped his head." She tipped one monkey over. Now she saw four monkeys standing. "Where did one go?" she asked. "It fell down," she said. She sang again. One more monkey fell. Now there were three.

Madison stopped and had to think. Each time she sang, one monkey fell. Each time, the number got one smaller. Three monkeys, then two, then one. She sang the last verse. The last monkey fell. Zero monkeys were standing. All five were lying down. "It gets one smaller each time," she whispered.

She set the five monkeys up again. She sang the song again from the start. One monkey fell, then another. She laughed at the pile. A library helper walked by. "That song is my favorite too," the helper said. Madison pointed at her monkeys. "Watch," she said. "One falls, and one less is left." She pushed the next monkey over.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Charlotte was playing blocks with her brother Sam. Grandma came in with a small bag. "This is for you, Charlotte," she said.

Inside was a new cup. It had a yellow bee on it. Charlotte held it up high. "My bee cup!" she said. Grandma smiled and went to paint at her table.

Sam looked at the cup too. Charlotte let him hold it. "Your turn," she said. "Now my turn." They took turns, back and forth. Then Grandma fell asleep in her chair. She was tired.

Charlotte looked at Grandma. She had not said her words yet. She ran back to the chair. She tapped Grandma's hand softly. Grandma opened her eyes.

"Thank you for my cup, Grandma," said Charlotte.

Grandma hugged her tight. "You are welcome, sweet girl," she said. Charlotte held her bee cup all the way to snack time.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Sarah stood in the bathroom. She wanted to wash her hands all by herself. "Can I do it?" she asked her dad. "Yes," said Dad. "I will turn the water for you."

Dad turned the red tap a tiny bit. The water ran warm. Dad held his own hand under it first. "Warm is good," he said. "Hot water can hurt. Only a grown-up touches the taps." Sarah watched the warm water. She put her hands in. The soap got bubbly. She rubbed and rubbed.

Then they heard a noise outside. A big truck went by. "The park!" said Sarah. She could see the swings from the window. "Can we go?" "Yes," said Dad. They walked to the door. Sarah reached up. She held her dad's hand. The road was in front of them. Sarah stopped at the edge. They looked left. They looked right. Then they walked across together.

At the park, Sarah ran to the swing. "I held your hand on the road," she said. Dad smiled. "You did," he said. "Now swing high, Sarah!" Sarah pumped her legs. The swing went up and up. "Watch me, Dad!" she called.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Emilia woke up from her nap. She was not asleep anymore. She wanted a bath right away.

Mama was in the kitchen. She filled a cup with water for Emilia to drink. Emilia tugged Mama's shirt. "Bath now, please!"

Mama turned on the bath water. Emilia tried to climb in fast. "Wait," said Mama. She held Emilia's hand. "A grown-up checks the bath water first. We make sure it is not too hot."

Mama put her hand in the water. Steam went up, up, up. "Too hot," said Mama. She added some cold water. She checked again with her hand. "Now it is just right."

Emilia put in her little foot. The water felt warm and nice. She splashed and laughed. Later Mama helped her get dressed in soft pajamas.

Then Daddy called on the phone. "Bath time went well?" he asked.

"Yes," said Emilia. "Mama checked the water with her hand."

After that, they ate bread and honey. Then Mama helped Emilia sweep crumbs from the floor. Emilia held the little broom with both hands.

She swept the crumbs into a small pile. "I did it!" said Emilia. Mama clapped.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Elijah sat in the big waiting chair. His feet did not touch the floor. He was waiting for his very first haircut. "I don't want one," he whispered to Dad. "My hair might fall off and never come back."

Dad laughed a little. "Come and sit with me. We can watch." A man sat in the salon chair. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down, dark bits on the bright floor. Then a boy got up from the chair. His hair was short now. "See," said Dad. "Look at that lady there. Her hair was cut last month. It is growing back already."

Elijah looked. The lady had little soft hairs on her head. New hairs! So hair comes back. "Okay," said Elijah. "My turn. But save the bits for the birds." The hairdresser smiled and held the broom. "The birds can have them," she said. Elijah climbed up into the big chair, way up high. Snip, snip. He watched his own dark bits fall. Then he made a tiny haircut for his teddy, too, snipping with two fingers, snip snip snip.

story:
Zoey wanted to tell Grandma her age. Grandma was coming today. Mom asked, "How old are you, Zoey?" Zoey held up her fingers. She looked at her hand. She did not know the word.

So Zoey tried. She held up one finger. "One!" she said. Mom shook her head and smiled. "Not one," said Mom. Zoey held up two fingers. "Two!" Mom shook her head again. "Keep trying," said Mom. "Take your time." Zoey tried three. Three little fingers went up in the air. "Three!" she said.

"Yes!" said Mom. "You are three." Zoey laughed and jumped. Then the door opened. Grandma came in with a big hug. "How old are you now?" Grandma asked. Zoey held up three fingers, nice and tall. "I am three!" she said. Grandma clapped. "Three is a special age," said Grandma. "Let us eat a snack and draw a picture together." Zoey sat at the table. She drew one circle, two circles, three. "One, two, three," she counted. Then she counted her grapes too. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Grandma counted with her, slow and easy, all the way to the end.

story: Grace held her dad's hand in the school hallway. The floor was shiny and squeaky. Squeak, squeak, went her shoes. A boy stood by the big doors. story:
Milan was at the park with his dad. He saw a big red strawberry in the picnic basket. He wanted it so much. His eyes were looking at it. His ears heard the birds sing. His nose smelled the sweet berry.

Milan took a bite. "Yum! So sweet!" he said. Then he had a funny idea. What if he held his nose closed? He squeezed his nose with his fingers. He took another bite. "Oh no!" he said. "It tastes plain now! Where did the sweet go?"

Dad laughed. "Try again with your nose open." Milan let go of his nose. He took a bite. The sweet taste came back! "My nose helps me taste!" said Milan. He touched the bumpy strawberry skin with his finger. Then he waved his arms like a big lucky elephant. "I know a trick now!" he said. "Watch me, Dad!" He squeezed his nose again and giggled.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Maria went to Miss Kim's music studio. She saw a big drum on the floor. "Can I play it?" Maria asked. "Yes," said Miss Kim. "Let's build a song together. You tap, and I tap too."

Maria tapped the drum. Boom! Boom! The room felt loud and hot from all the drumming. Miss Kim played a lion song, loud and strong. Maria tapped along. The song went fast, then slow, then it stopped.

Mama and Miss Kim clapped their hands. Clap, clap, clap! Maria just stood there. She looked at Miss Kim. Miss Kim bent down low at her waist. Maria did the same thing. She bent down low, too. Clap, clap, clap went Mama's hands again. Maria smiled big. Every time they clapped, she bowed again. Bow, clap. Bow, clap. "Again!" said Maria, and she bowed one more time.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Abigail woke up and saw snow. The whole park was white and wide. "No school today!" said Mama. "Get your warm coat."

Abigail put on her boots. She put on her hat. She ran out the door fast. But she forgot her mittens.

At the park, Abigail made a big snowball. Then her fingers felt cold. They felt like ice. "Ow," she said. Her hands hurt too much to clap.

"I need my mittens," she said. She ran back home. Mama helped her put them on. "Warm hands now," said Mama.

Abigail went back to the park. She rolled and rolled. Her fingers stayed warm inside the mittens. Her coat kept her body warm. Her boots kept her feet dry.

Then she saw something in the snow. A little green frog sat by the pond! "Hello, frog," said Abigail. The frog jumped one time, then two times.

Abigail clapped her warm hands. "Best snow day ever," she said. The frog blinked at her, and she laughed and laughed.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ivy had to wait at the doctor's office. She was feeling grumpy because her teddy was missing. "Where is Ted?" she asked Mom. The nurse said, "Maybe he fell in the back room." That room was dark. Ivy peeked in. It was hard to see in the dark. She could only see shadows.

Ivy stood still and listened with her ears. She heard no teddy sounds. She sniffed with her nose. She smelled soap and bandages, no teddy. Then the nurse said, "I will turn on the light for you." She clicked the switch. The lamp came on.

Now Ivy could see everything. Ted was on a small chair! She ran and grabbed him. She hugged his soft fur with her hands. The nurse gave her a sweet sticker. Ivy put it on her tongue and tasted the shiny paper. "Yuck," she said. Everyone laughed, and Ivy laughed too. "Good team," said Mom, holding her hand.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Kayden ran onto the big green field. "The game is starting!" he shouted. Mom held his hand. Grandpa carried a red blanket. The sun was warm on Kayden's face. The weather was good for a game.

The players kicked the ball. Everybody cheered. Kayden clapped his hands. "Go, go, go!" he yelled. One team kicked the ball into the net. Boom! The crowd jumped up. Then the other team kicked the ball in too. Boom! Kayden stomped his feet with joy.

The whistle blew. The game was over. Kayden tugged Mom's sleeve. "Who won?" he asked. Mom looked at the big board. Both numbers were the same. Two and two. "Nobody won today," she said. "The same score is called a tie."

"A tie!" said Kayden. He held up two fingers on each hand. "Same, same!" He laughed. Grandpa picked him up high. Kayden dreamed of kicking the ball in the net himself one day. "Kick it far!" he called to the players leaving the field.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Isaac ran to the backyard with a big basket. "Today I cook soup!" he said. Daddy had carrots from the market. Isaac pulled one out. It had dirt all over it. "Yuck!" said Isaac. "Can we eat dirty carrots?"

"No," said Daddy. "Cooks rinse dirt off carrots first." Isaac ran to the sink. He turned the water on. He scrubbed the carrot with his hands. The dirt washed away. The water turned brown, then clear. "Look!" said Isaac. "The carrot is clean and orange now!"

He rinsed every carrot, one by one. He rinsed a potato too. Then Daddy cut them up. Daddy put the pot on the stove. Isaac watched from his chair. Soon the soup went pop, pop, pop. "Mmm," said Mommy at the table. "My name for this soup is Isaac's Special." Isaac grinned big. "I rinsed it myself!"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Luke ran into the storytime room. Today he would get his first library card! It had his name on it. Luke wore his round red hat because it was a big day.

A girl put her book on the wrong shelf. The librarian picked it up. She turned the book sideways. "See this little label on the spine?" she said. Luke looked. The label said a letter and a number. The librarian put the book under the same letter on the shelf. It fit right there, like a seed fits in a hole.

Luke picked out a book about a big red truck. He looked at the spine. "This one lives over there," he said. He put it back in its spot. Then he took it to the desk.

The librarian smiled. "One book for Luke," she said. Luke held his card up high. "My first book!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Violet was on the little swim team. The pool was blue and cool. It smelled like sunscreen. "Kick, kick, kick," said the water in her ears.

Today was the relay race. Violet stood in the middle of the deck. She did not know where to stand. She looked left. She looked right. The other kids were in lines. Violet wondered where her line was.

"Coach Kim," she said. "Where do I stand?" Coach Kim smiled. "Come with me. I teach the team and help you learn the game." Coach Kim pointed to the wall. "Stand here, next to the ladder. When your friend taps your hand, you jump in and swim fast."

Violet stood by the ladder. She waited. The water went splish, splash, splish. Her friend Ada swam close. Ada tapped Violet's hand. Violet jumped in. She kicked her legs. She paddled her arms. She touched the other side!

"Where do I stand?" asked her friend Milo. He looked confused, just like she had. Violet pointed to the ladder. "Coach Kim teaches the team," she said. "She shows us where to go. Stand here, and tap my hand when I swim back." Milo smiled and got ready.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Everly stood at the big desk in the library. She wanted her very own library card. The librarian smiled and typed on her computer. "Here it is," she said. "Your first card, Everly."

Everly held the card with two hands. It had her name on it. Then she heard a loud voice from the other room. "Storytime!" the librarian called out. Children ran to sit on the rug. Everly hid behind her mommy's legs.

"What is storytime?" Everly asked. Mommy said, "Let's go see." The librarian sat in a small chair. She opened a big funny book. "Achoo!" she read, and made a silly face. All the children laughed. Everly peeked. Then she sat right down on the rug too.

After the story, Everly picked a book about a bunny. She gave the librarian her new card. The librarian stamped the book. "Bye-bye, bunny book," Everly said, and hugged it tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Mackenzie turned four today. Her whole family came to the bowling alley. Grandma, Dad, and her friend Zoe were there too.

Dad blew up a big red balloon. He puffed and puffed until it was round. "This one is for you," he said. Mackenzie held the string tight.

The party store balloons on the wall floated up high. They sat near the ceiling all day. Mackenzie looked at them. Then she looked at her red balloon. She wanted to see it fly up too.

She let go of the string. "Fly, balloon, fly!" she said. "Fly, balloon, fly!" But the balloon did not fly up. It went down, down, down. It landed softly on the floor by her party shoes.

Zoe picked it up and handed it back. "It likes the floor," said Zoe. Mackenzie laughed. She let go again. Down it went, down, down, down, right onto the bowling lane.

The red balloon rolled slowly into the gutter. A man came and helped get it out. Then Dad gave Mackenzie a balloon from the party store. That one floated up, up, up.

"Happy birthday, Mackenzie!" said Grandma. Mackenzie munched a salty pretzel. Then she rolled her ball down the lane and watched every pin fall down.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Zayn stood on the baseball diamond. He wanted to hit the ball far. The sun was bright. His teammate Mia was up first. She swung the bat. She missed the ball.

Mia's face looked sad. But then the whole team clapped. "Try again, Mia!" they called. Mia smiled. She swung again, and she hit the ball! It went deep into the grass. Everyone cheered loud.

Then it was Zayn's turn. He swung the bat. He missed too. "Do you feel sad now?" Mia asked him. "No," said Zayn. "I hear you cheering!" The team clapped for him. Zayn took a big breath. He swung again. Crack! The ball flew. Mia jumped up and down. "Run, Zayn, run!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Emily wanted her bedtime story. She ran to the bookshelf. But Daddy was still in the kitchen.

Emily looked at the book by herself. The cover had words on it. She pointed at the letters. "Cat," she said slowly. The picture showed a cat. The words said cat too.

She opened the front of the book. "This way," she whispered. She turned one page. Then another page. She hummed a little song and waited for Daddy.

Daddy came in with warm milk. "Read the words," said Emily. Daddy read them. The words told about a curly cat with soft fur.

"Words tell us things," said Emily. "Like the sign at the store says STOP." Daddy smiled. "Yes. Words are on boxes and signs too."

Emily looked at the milk box. There were little words on it. She pointed at them. Then she snuggled down and turned to the last page. "Good night, curly cat," she said.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Beatrice woke up and saw white snow. "No school today!" said Mama. "Snow day!"

Beatrice put on her red coat. She put on her puffy mittens. She ran to the big sledding hill. Dad pulled the sled up, up, up. Then down they went, fast and bumpy. Beatrice laughed and laughed.

Then Beatrice lay down in the snow. She swept her arms. She swept her legs. She stood up to look. "Oh no!" Her boot made a big smudge on her snow shape. "Try again," said Dad. "You lie down and sweep, then I help you up." So Beatrice lay in a different spot. She swept her arms and legs. Dad pulled her hands, and she popped up without touching the snow. There it was! "It looks like an angel!" said Beatrice. "A snow angel," said Dad. Beatrice flopped down again right away. "I need ten more!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story: Rowan's basket fell over in the backyard. All his picture cards spilled out on the grass. Rowan wanted to find his dog card, but there were so many cards. "Too many," he said. Dad sat down next to him. "We can make piles," Dad said. Rowan put the dog card down. Then he put the cat card on top of it. Then the bird card. "These are all animals," Dad said. Rowan found more animal cards. A fish. A cow. The animal pile grew big. Then Rowan found a ball card. It was not an animal. He started a new pile for toys. The ball went there. The drum went there. The kite went there too. Rowan found a picture of an apple. "Apple is a food," he said. He made a third pile for foods. The bread card went there. The banana card went there. The cheese card went there. Now the grass had three neat piles. Rowan looked at the animal pile. He found his dog card right away. "Woof," said Rowan, holding it up high. Dad laughed and clapped. Then Dad brought out a frozen pop from the house. He handed it to Rowan. Rowan sat on the warm grass and licked it. "Best pile day ever," said Dad.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Everly sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She looked around with her eyes. She saw a poster on the wall. It had a happy face on it.

Then Everly heard a sound. Beep, beep! It came from down the hall. She used her ears to hear it. The room smelled like soap, and she smelled it with her nose. The nurse gave her a sticker that felt bumpy. Everly touched it with her fingers.

Now it was time for her checkup. "Open wide," said the doctor. Everly opened her mouth. The doctor looked at her tongue. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Everly said, "Ahh!" She could taste a little yucky taste in her mouth.

Then the doctor said, "Time for one small poke." Everly did not want a poke. She squeezed her eyes shut tight. Now she could not see the doctor. Now she could not see her mama. She could not see anything at all!

But the doctor still saw Everly. The poke came anyway. It was quick. It was small. "All done," said the doctor. Everly opened her eyes. She could see again! Her mama held out a cookie from her bag. Everly took a bite. It tasted sweet. "That was fast," said Everly. "Can I read the poster now?" The doctor laughed and pointed to the happy face.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Livia could not find her spotted bunny at daycare. "Where did you go, Bunny?" she asked. Miss Ana helped her look. They peeked under the table. No bunny. They looked in the toy box. No bunny. Livia felt like crying a little. "It is okay to feel sad," said Miss Ana. "We will keep looking."

Then Livia saw Tommy's big coat on the hook. The coat had a pocket. The pocket was bumpy and round. She reached in and pulled out her bunny. "My bunny was inside the pocket!" she said. Tommy laughed. "I put my snacks in there," he said. "Maybe Bunny wanted a snack too."

Miss Ana smiled. "Livia, will you speak at circle time and tell everyone?" Livia hugged Bunny tight. "Yes! Bunny was hiding in the coat, inside the pocket!" Then Bunny got a turn on the slide, right before snack time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story: Anna had a little drum. It sat in the school band room. Miss Polly said, "Play the bumpy song today." Anna tried. Boing, boom, splat. The song came out wrong. Anna frowned. "I'm afraid I can't do it," she said. "It's too hard." Tom laughed, not mean, just a little. "My song was hard too," he said. "Now watch me!" He played his song all the way through. Anna wanted to know how he did it. "I just played a little bit every day," said Tom. So Anna played her drum a little bit. Then she stopped and had a cookie. The next day she played a little bit again. Boing, boom. The next day, boom, boom, ting. Every day she played some more. One morning Anna sat at her drum. She took a big breath. Boom, boom, ting, boom! The song came out right, all the way to the end. Tom clapped. Miss Polly clapped. Anna bowed and hit one last boom.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jaxon ran to the park. He saw a big red truck in the sand. It was not his truck. It was Ben's truck.

Jaxon wanted it so much. He grabbed the truck fast. Ben began to cry. His face went sad and red.

Jaxon looked at Ben. He looked at the truck. Maybe the truck was Ben's very own? Jaxon gave the truck back. "Can I have a turn?" he asked.

Ben wiped his eyes. "Yes," said Ben. "Can I have my turtle after?" Jaxon nodded. First Jaxon pushed the truck. The wheels went round and round. Then he gave it to Ben. Ben made the turtle splash in a puddle. The water went splash, splash, splash. Then Ben handed the turtle to Jaxon.

A big kid ran up. He reached for the truck with one strong hand. "Ask first," said Ben. The big kid stopped. "Can I play too?" he asked. "Yes!" said Jaxon.

They all sat in the sand. Truck, turtle, truck, turtle, round and round. Jaxon smiled. "This is a good game," he said. "Ask, and then take a turn."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Jayden was at the park for his birthday. There was a big cake on the table. Mom set candles on top. Jayden counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four." Then he stopped. He looked at Mom. "Am I four this year?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "You are five now. One candle for each year."

So Jayden knew what to do. "We need one more candle!" Mom smiled and put it on. Now there were five candles, all the same size. Dad lit them with a match, far from Jayden's hands.

A little wind blew by. One flame wiggled. Then all the flames bent the same way. "Quick, make a wish!" said Dad. Jayden closed his eyes. "I wish for this same cake next year," he said. Then he blew, and the candles went out. "Did my wish go into the smoke?" he asked. Grandma laughed. "Maybe it spells yes in the sky."
